results.authors: Mas JL, Derumeaux G, Guillon B, et al.
results.key_finding: In patients aged 16 to 60 with a recent stroke attributed to a PFO with an atrial septal aneurysm or a large shunt, closure plus antiplatelet therapy led to no recurrent strokes versus 14 (6.0%) with antiplatelet therapy alone over a mean 5.3 years.
results.title: Patent Foramen Ovale Closure or Anticoagulation vs. Antiplatelets after Stroke (CLOSE)

results.authors: Saver JL, Carroll JD, Thaler DE, et al.
results.key_finding: In adults aged 18 to 60 with cryptogenic ischemic stroke and a PFO, closure reduced recurrent ischemic stroke over a median 5.9 years (HR 0.55); the reduction was larger for recurrent strokes of undetermined mechanism (HR 0.38).
results.title: Long-Term Outcomes of Patent Foramen Ovale Closure or Medical Therapy after Stroke (RESPECT)

results.authors: Kent DM, Ruthazer R, Weimar C, et al.
results.key_finding: The RoPE score (0 to 10: absence of hypertension, diabetes, prior stroke or TIA and smoking, cortical infarct, and younger age) estimates the probability that a PFO found in cryptogenic stroke is pathogenic; higher scores carry a higher PFO-attributable fraction.
results.title: An index to identify stroke-related vs incidental patent foramen ovale in cryptogenic stroke

results.authors: Messe SR, Gronseth GS, Kent DM, et al.
results.key_finding: AAN practice advisory: in patients aged 60 or younger with an embolic-appearing infarct, a PFO and no other mechanism identified after a thorough evaluation, clinicians may recommend closure after discussing the potential benefits and risks.
results.title: Practice advisory update summary: Patent foramen ovale and secondary stroke prevention

output.summary: Randomized trials in patients aged 60 or younger with a PFO-associated stroke show fewer recurrent strokes after closure than with medical therapy alone, with the largest benefit in large shunts or atrial septal aneurysm; the RoPE score estimates how likely the PFO is causal.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not dismiss this presentation as migraine with aura or a functional visual disturbance because of the young age and absent vascular risk factors: the persistent hemianopia with hemibody sensory loss is a stroke until imaging shows otherwise.
Do not give IV thrombolysis for this wake-up stroke: FLAIR is already positive and CT perfusion shows no salvageable penumbra by EXTEND criteria.
Do not take the patient to thrombectomy for the distal left P2-P3 occlusion: medium vessel occlusions have no graded thrombectomy indication.

Do not settle on a PFO-associated mechanism treated with antiplatelet therapy alone before imaging the tender left leg and monitoring the rhythm: a venous thrombus calls for anticoagulation, and atrial fibrillation would change the mechanism.

Do not start or restart antihypertensive treatment in the first 48 to 72 hours for blood pressure below 220/120 mmHg in a patient who receives neither IV thrombolysis nor thrombectomy and has no comorbid indication; it does not prevent death or dependency (AHA/ASA 2026, COR 3: No Benefit).
required_recommendations: Establish last known well (23:00 the previous evening, 8 hours before arrival at 07:00) and the NIHSS (4).
Obtain non-contrast CT head first to exclude intracranial hemorrhage before any reperfusion decision.

IV thrombolysis: do not give. FLAIR is positive, which closes the DWI-FLAIR limb; he woke within 9 hours of the sleep midpoint (about 02:40, 4 hours 20 minutes before arrival) and is not a thrombectomy candidate, but CT perfusion does not meet EXTEND criteria (core 22 mL, mismatch 3 mL, ratio 1.14). Thrombectomy: not indicated; the left P2-P3 occlusion is a medium vessel occlusion with no graded indication (ESCAPE-MeVO and DISTAL showed no benefit).
Admit to a stroke unit with continuous cardiac monitoring (telemetry) for at least the first 24 hours.

Treat the left calf deep vein thrombosis with therapeutic anticoagulation for at least 3 months (for example apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily), started once follow-up brain imaging excludes hemorrhagic transformation and timed to the infarct size (about 4.8 cm across several PCA branches: defer for several days rather than start within 48 hours); give aspirin from the first 24 to 48 hours until then and stop it when anticoagulation starts, which replaces antiplatelet therapy. Review the duration beyond 3 months with the heterozygous factor V Leiden result.

Discuss PFO closure with cardiology after the acute phase: age 34, RoPE score 9 and a large shunt with a demonstrated venous source make the PFO very likely causal (AAN 2020 practice advisory supports offering closure after shared decision-making).
If inpatient monitoring finds no atrial fibrillation, arrange prolonged ambulatory rhythm monitoring (30-day event monitor or implantable loop recorder) before PFO closure.
Counsel on venous thrombosis prevention for future long-haul travel (mobilization, hydration, compression stockings) and offer factor V Leiden counselling to first-degree relatives.

Start atorvastatin 80 mg daily: LDL 108 mg/dL after a non-cardioembolic ischaemic stroke without known coronary disease meets the AHA/ASA 2021 secondary prevention indication (COR 1, SPARCL), although the mechanism is paradoxical embolism through the PFO rather than atherosclerosis; target LDL below 70 mg/dL.

key_clinical_evidence: Right homonymous hemianopia with right hemibody sensory loss and alexia without agraphia localise to the left PCA territory: left occipital cortex, left posterolateral thalamus and the left splenium, which disconnects the intact right visual cortex from the left language areas.
Young age and absent vascular risk factors do not exclude ischemic stroke; the CT hypodensity, the P2-P3 thrombus on CTA and the DWI lesion make the deficit an infarct.

Wake-up stroke: FLAIR is positive, so the DWI-FLAIR limb is closed; the sleep midpoint is about 02:40, 4 hours 20 minutes before arrival, and the patient is not an EVT candidate, so CTP does not meet EXTEND criteria (core 22 mL, mismatch 3 mL, ratio 1.14).
The left P2-P3 occlusion is a medium vessel occlusion with no graded thrombectomy indication.

Paradoxical embolism needs a venous thrombus and a right-to-left shunt with no better arterial or cardiac source: the duplex shows an acute left calf DVT (anticipated by the D-dimer of 1820 and calf tenderness after a 7.5-hour flight), the bubble study shows a large PFO shunt, and CTA, ECG, Holter and echocardiography show no other mechanism.
RoPE score 9 (age 30-39: 4; no hypertension, diabetes, prior stroke or TIA, or smoking: 4; cortical infarct: 1) gives a high probability that the PFO is causal.
Heterozygous factor V Leiden raises the risk of venous thrombosis and helps explain the DVT after the flight; it does not enter the RoPE score and is not an arterial thrombophilia.

AHA/ASA 2026 sequencing: glucose is checked before thrombolysis, but routine CBC and coagulation results are not awaited without a reason to expect abnormality; ECG and troponin do not delay reperfusion, and CTA and CTP do not wait for creatinine.

clinical_pearls: Left PCA territory infarction causes a right homonymous hemianopia and, when the thalamogeniculate branches are involved, right-sided sensory loss from the left thalamus.
PFO-associated (paradoxical) embolism is a leading mechanism of otherwise unexplained stroke in young adults; an agitated-saline study detects the shunt and leg venous imaging looks for the source.
Prolonged immobility on a long-haul flight provokes calf DVT; a PFO lets venous emboli cross into the arterial circulation.
Heterozygous factor V Leiden is the most prevalent inherited thrombophilia in Europeans and raises venous thrombosis risk several-fold.
The RoPE score assigns a high probability that a PFO is causal when the patient is young, has no vascular risk factors and has a cortical infarct.
Alexia without agraphia (reading impaired, writing preserved) is a classic left PCA syndrome due to disconnection of the right visual cortex from the left language areas through the splenium.
metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle: 34-year-old man with no vascular risk factors presenting with right homonymous hemianopia on waking after a transatlantic flight. Young age and visual symptoms invite a migraine or functional explanation. The correct path confirms a left PCA infarct, closes both extended-window thrombolysis limbs (FLAIR positive; CT perfusion without salvageable penumbra), recognises the P2-P3 occlusion as a medium vessel occlusion, and then builds the paradoxical-embolism mechanism: calf DVT on duplex (anticipated by D-dimer and calf tenderness), a large PFO shunt on the bubble study, no atrial fibrillation on monitoring, and heterozygous factor V Leiden as a venous risk factor.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Young PFO-associated stroke; requires the wake-up thrombolysis decision on both limbs, venous duplex, agitated-saline echocardiography and rhythm monitoring before attributing the stroke to the PFO; the red herring is the migraine anchor from young age and isolated visual symptoms.
metadata.revision_reason: Independent Reviewer 2 stroke audit: NCCT and CTA separated; MRI optional; CTP routed only to two extended-window cases; routine MRA/TCD/duplex duplication removed; acute labs carry explicit do-not-delay rules; EEG retained for one seizure-mimic case

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Marco Ferreira is a 34-year-old right-handed man with no significant past medical history who presents to the emergency department at 07:00 after acute onset of right-sided visual loss noticed upon waking this morning. He describes being unable to see anything to the right in both eyes. He also endorses mild numbness of the right face and right arm. His partner confirms he was neurologically normal when they went to bed at 23:00; he woke at 06:20 with the deficit already present. He returned 48 hours ago from a transatlantic flight from Lisbon to Boston, approximately 7.5 hours in economy class with minimal mobility. He did not get up during the flight and slept for most of it. He has no history of hypertension, diabetes, cardiac disease, or prior neurological events. His partner notes he had been rubbing his eyes and shaking his head on waking, wondering if it would pass. On arrival in the ED he reports the visual loss is persistent and unchanged. He denies chest pain, palpitations, dyspnea, or leg swelling, though on directed questioning he admits to mild left calf aching since the flight, which he attributed to 'economy class syndrome.' He has no known family history of stroke. A paternal aunt had an unprovoked DVT at age 42. He takes no medications. He denies tobacco use and illicit drugs. Last known well is 23:00 the prior evening, 8 hours before arrival.
